What is CI/CD?.exp: Introduction to Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment.
What is CI/CD?.code: CI/CD pipeline concepts, benefits, and the DevOps lifecycle.

Build Automation.code: Compilation, dependency resolution, asset bundling, artifact creation.

What is CI/CD: CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment. It is a method of frequently delivering apps to customers by introducing automation into the stages of app development. CI/CD bridges the gap between development and operations teams by automating build, test, and deployment processes. Continuous Integration ensures every code change is automatically built and tested, catching bugs early. Continuous Delivery extends CI by automatically deploying code to production-like environments for testing. Continuous Deployment takes it further — every change that passes all stages of the pipeline is automatically released to production.
Benefits of CI/CD:
Adopting CI/CD brings several key benefits:
  • Faster releases — automate manual steps to ship code multiple times a day
  • Reduced risk — catch bugs early with automated testing in every commit
  • Higher quality — consistent testing and code analysis standards
  • Developer productivity — less time spent on manual deployments and debugging
  • Auditability — every change is tracked, tested, and logged
  • Team confidence — automated validation means safer deployments
Companies practicing CI/CD deploy code 208x more frequently than those that don't (DORA State of DevOps report).
Pipeline Architecture:
A CI/CD pipeline is a series of automated steps that code goes through from commit to deployment. The typical stages are:
  • Source — code is pushed to version control (Git)
  • Build — code is compiled and dependencies are resolved
  • Test — automated tests (unit, integration, e2e) are run
  • Analyze — static analysis, linting, and security scanning
  • Package — artifacts (binaries, containers) are built and stored
  • Deploy — artifacts are deployed to staging or production
Each stage must pass before the next begins — this is called a gated pipeline. Modern pipelines run stages in parallel where possible for speed.

GitHub Actions.code: Workflows, jobs, steps, actions, matrix builds, triggers.

Automated Testing in CI.code: Unit tests, integration tests, linting, code coverage, quality gates.

Automated Testing:
Testing is the heart of CI. Every pipeline should run multiple levels of tests:
  • Unit tests — test individual functions and methods (fastest, most coverage)
  • Integration tests — test interactions between components (database, API, services)
  • End-to-end tests — test the full system from user perspective (slowest, least coverage)
The test pyramid suggests many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few e2e tests. Tests should be deterministic — always pass or fail the same way given the same code. Flaky tests undermine CI trust.
Code Quality & Linting:
Automated code quality checks are essential in CI/CD. These include:
  • Linters — ESLint (JS/TS), Ruff/Flake8 (Python), Clippy (Rust), golangci-lint (Go)
  • Formatters — Prettier, Black, gofmt, rustfmt
  • Static analysis — SonarQube, CodeQL, Coverity
  • Type checking — TypeScript (tsc), mypy (Python), Flow
These checks should fail the pipeline if thresholds are not met (e.g., code coverage < 80%, lint errors, type errors). Many teams enforce formatting with pre-commit hooks and reserve CI for deeper analysis.

CI Pipeline Design.code: Pipeline stages, parallel execution, caching, failure handling.

Build Automation:
Build automation is the process of automating the compilation of source code into executable artifacts. Every commit should produce a build to verify the code compiles correctly. Common build tools by language:
  • JavaScript/TypeScript — npm, yarn, pnpm, vite, webpack
  • Java — Maven, Gradle
  • Python — setuptools, poetry, pipenv
  • Go — go build
  • Rust — cargo build
  • C/C++ — CMake, Make, GCC
The build stage should be fast (under 5 minutes) to provide quick feedback. Cache dependencies between builds to speed up execution.

Branching Strategies:
CI/CD pipelines work hand-in-hand with branching strategies. Common approaches include:
  • GitFlow — main, develop, feature, release, and hotfix branches. Good for scheduled releases but complex.
  • GitHub Flow — single main branch with feature branches and pull requests. Simpler, ideal for continuous deployment.
  • Trunk-based Development — short-lived feature branches merged to main multiple times a day. Best for CI/CD with automated testing.
CI/CD pipelines typically trigger on push to specific branches (e.g., main) and on pull requests for validation before merge.
Git Hooks:
Git hooks are scripts that run automatically before or after Git events like commit, push, or merge. They are stored in the .git/hooks directory and can enforce policies locally before code reaches the remote repository. Common CI/CD use cases include:
  • pre-commit — run linters, format code, check for secrets
  • pre-push — run unit tests before pushing
  • commit-msg — enforce conventional commit format
  • post-merge — install new dependencies after pulling
Tools like Husky and lint-staged make managing hooks easier across teams.
Pull Request Workflows:
Pull requests (PRs) are at the heart of modern CI/CD. A typical PR workflow:
  1. Developer creates a feature branch, commits changes, and pushes
  2. PR is opened, triggering a CI pipeline that runs tests and analysis
  3. PR checks report status (pass/fail) directly in the PR view
  4. Team reviews code; additional commits trigger re-runs
  5. Once approved and all checks pass, the PR is merged
  6. Merge triggers a CD pipeline to build and deploy
Tools like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Azure DevOps integrate PR checks natively with status badges and required checks.

Configuration Management:
Configuration management tools maintain consistent system state across environments:
  • Ansible — agentless, push-based, YAML playbooks. Great for app deployment and server configuration.
  • Chef — Ruby-based DSL, pull-based with Chef Client and Server. Good for large-scale server fleets.
  • Puppet — declarative DSL, pull-based. Strong in enterprise environments.
In CI/CD, run config management as part of the deployment stage to ensure servers match the desired state after deployment.
Policy as Code:
Policy as Code (PaC) enforces rules automatically in the pipeline:
  • Open Policy Agent (OPA) — general-purpose policy engine. Enforce rules like "all S3 buckets must be encrypted" before apply.
  • Sentinel — HashiCorp's policy framework for Terraform and Vault.
  • Checkov — static analysis for IaC to find misconfigurations (open ports, hardcoded secrets).
  • Conftest — test configuration files against OPA policies in CI.
PaC shifts security left — catching policy violations before infrastructure is provisioned.
Terraform in CI/CD:
Applying Infrastructure as Code (IaC) through CI/CD brings infrastructure changes under the same governance as application changes. Terraform CI/CD best practices:
  • Run terraform fmt and terraform validate in CI to check formatting and syntax
  • Use terraform plan in PRs to show infrastructure changes without applying them
  • Store state remotely (S3, Terraform Cloud) with state locking
  • Apply only after PR approval and plan review
  • Use workspaces or directories for environment separation
The terraform plan output in a PR comment is one of the most valuable CI/CD practices for infrastructure teams.

Infrastructure as Code.code: Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi; declarative vs imperative IaC.

Configuration Management.code: Ansible, Puppet, Chef; idempotency, desired state.

Secrets Management.code: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, encrypted environment variables.

Logging.code: ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), Loki, Fluentd.

Metrics.code: Prometheus, Grafana, metrics types (counter, gauge, histogram).

Tracing.code: Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry; trace context propagation.

Alerting.code: Alertmanager, PagerDuty, on-call rotations, escalation policies.

SLOs & SLIs.code: Defining reliability targets, error budgets, burn rates.

Incident Response:
When a CI/CD pipeline failure or production incident occurs, a structured response process is essential:
  1. Detect — automated monitoring and alerts detect the failure
  2. Stop the bleeding — rollback the deployment or block the pipeline
  3. Triage — determine severity, impact, and affected teams
  4. Investigate — review logs, metrics, and pipeline output to find root cause
  5. Remediate — fix the issue and push the fix through the same CI/CD pipeline
  6. Review — post-mortem to prevent recurrence
CI/CD pipelines themselves should be treated as critical infrastructure with their own monitoring, redundancy, and incident response plans.
Pipeline Metrics:
Track these key metrics to measure CI/CD pipeline health:
  • Pipeline duration — time from commit to deployment. Target: under 15 minutes total.
  • Build failure rate — percentage of builds that fail. Target: under 10%.
  • Deployment frequency — how often you deploy to production. Elite teams deploy multiple times per day.
  • Mean Time to Recover (MTTR) — time from detecting a failure to recovery. Target: under 1 hour.
  • Change failure rate — percentage of deployments causing incidents. Target: under 5%.
These are the DORA metrics — the industry standard for measuring DevOps and CI/CD performance.
Pipeline Notifications:
Keep teams informed about pipeline status with automated notifications:
  • Slack/Discord — send messages on failure, success, or deployment events. Include links to the pipeline run.
  • Email — send summaries for failed pipelines or approval requests
  • Status badges — embed pipeline status (passing/failing) in README files
  • PR comments — post test results, coverage changes, and deployment URLs directly in PRs
Most CI/CD platforms have built-in notification integrations. Focus on actionable alerts — don't spam teams with every successful build.

DevSecOps.code: Shift-left security, automated scanning, compliance as code.

SAST & DAST:
Security testing should be integrated into every pipeline:
  • SAST (Static Application Security Testing) — analyzes source code for vulnerabilities without running it. Tools: SonarQube, CodeQL, Semgrep, Checkmarx. Runs early in the pipeline (build stage).
  • DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) — tests running applications for vulnerabilities. Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite. Runs against staging environments later in the pipeline.
SAST catches issues early (shift left), while DAST catches runtime vulnerabilities. Both should be gated — fail the pipeline on high-severity findings.
Secret Scanning:
Accidentally committing secrets (API keys, passwords, tokens) is one of the most common CI/CD security issues. Prevent and detect with:
  • Pre-commit hooks — tools like talisman, git-secrets, and detect-secrets scan before commits
  • CI scanning — GitHub Secret Scanning, GitLab Secret Detection, TruffleHog scan in the pipeline
  • Secret managers — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager
CI/CD configs should reference secrets from the CI platform's built-in secrets store (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, Jenkins credentials), never hardcode them.
SBOM & Supply Chain:
Software supply chain security is critical in 2026:
  • SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — a machine-readable inventory of all components in your software. Generated by tools like CycloneDX and Syft.
  • Dependency scanning — Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk automatically detect and update vulnerable dependencies
  • Artifact signing — sign container images and binaries with Cosign to verify authenticity
  • Attestations — create signed metadata about how and where artifacts were built
AI-generated code increases the importance of SBOM scanning. Every CI/CD pipeline should generate and verify SBOMs before deployment.

Supply Chain Security.code: SBOM, signed commits, dependency verification, SLSA framework.

Container Security.code: Image scanning, minimal base images, runtime security (Falco).

GitHub Actions: GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI/CD platform. Workflows are defined as YAML files in .github/workflows/. It offers deep GitHub integration, a large marketplace of pre-built actions, and supports Linux, macOS, Windows, and containers. Key concepts: workflows (automated processes), jobs (sets of steps), steps (individual tasks), runners (execution environments). GitHub provides free minutes for public repositories and paid minutes for private ones.
Jenkins: Jenkins is the most widely used open-source automation server. It supports hundreds of plugins for building, deploying, and automating projects. Jenkins pipelines can be defined as code using Jenkinsfile with Declarative or Scripted pipeline syntax. Strengths: extreme flexibility, massive plugin ecosystem, mature community. Weaknesses: requires server management, UI can feel dated, plugin compatibility issues. Best for complex enterprise environments needing fine-grained control.
CircleCI: CircleCI is a cloud-native CI/CD platform known for speed and reliability. Pipelines are configured in a .circleci/config.yml file. CircleCI supports parallelism, caching, and Orbs — reusable configuration packages that simplify complex pipelines. Key features: Docker layer caching, SSH debugging for troubleshooting, dynamic configuration via pipeline parameters, and optimized resource classes (CPU/RAM per job). CircleCI offers a generous free tier for individual developers and open-source projects.
Azure DevOps: Azure DevOps is Microsoft's full DevSecOps platform providing a complete toolchain: Azure Pipelines (CI/CD), Azure Boards (work tracking), Azure Repos (Git repos), Azure Artifacts (package management), and Azure Test Plans (testing). Azure Pipelines supports any language, platform, and cloud. Key strengths: deep Azure integration, deployment groups for multi-machine rollouts, Kubernetes integration, and YAML or classic editor pipeline definitions. Free tier includes 1,800 minutes per month.

GitLab Runners & Scaling:
GitLab Runners are the agents that execute CI/CD jobs. Types include:
  • Shared runners — GitLab-hosted, available to all projects (Linux, Windows, macOS)
  • Group runners — available to all projects in a group
  • Project runners — dedicated to a single project
  • Specific runners — locked to specific projects or tags
Scaling strategies: use Docker autoscaling with Docker Machine or Kubernetes with the GitLab Runner Helm chart to spin up runners dynamically based on job demand. GitLab Runner supports executors including Docker, Kubernetes, SSH, and VirtualBox.
GitLab CI/CD Overview: GitLab CI/CD is GitLab's built-in continuous integration, delivery, and deployment system. Pipelines are defined declaratively in a .gitlab-ci.yml file at the repository root. GitLab CI/CD is deeply integrated into the GitLab platform, providing a unified experience for source control, CI/CD, container registry, package registry, and deployment. Key strengths: single application for the entire DevOps lifecycle, built-in auto-scaling runners, review apps for per-branch environments, and a generous free tier for both public and private repositories.
GitLab CI Pipeline Configuration:
GitLab CI pipelines are defined in YAML with these core concepts:
  • Stages — groups of jobs that run in order (e.g., build, test, deploy). Jobs in the same stage run in parallel.
  • Jobs — define what to run (script, image, dependencies). Each job belongs to a stage.
  • Runners — agents that execute jobs. GitLab provides shared runners (Linux, Windows, macOS) and you can register your own.
  • Variables — environment variables for configuration. Can be set at project, group, or instance level.
  • Cache & Artifacts — cache speeds up dependency installs; artifacts pass build outputs between stages.
Example pipeline: lint → test → build → deploy. Jobs can run conditionally based on branch, tags, or changes to specific files.
GitLab Auto DevOps:
Auto DevOps is GitLab's zero-configuration CI/CD pipeline. When enabled, GitLab automatically detects your application language and builds a complete pipeline including:
  • Code quality analysis (SonarQube)
  • SAST and Dependency Scanning
  • Container scanning and DAST
  • License compliance review
  • Automatic deployment to staging and production
  • Review Apps (temporary environments per merge request)
  • Performance testing and browser testing
Auto DevOps uses a Dockerfile or buildpack to build your app. It's ideal for teams new to CI/CD who want instant value without writing pipeline config.

Rollback & Recovery:
Even the best pipelines can fail in production. CD systems must support fast, reliable rollback:
  • Automated rollback — if health checks fail after deployment, automatically revert to the last known-good version
  • Database rollbacks — use reversible migrations (up/down) to safely revert schema changes
  • Version pinning — always tag deployed versions (git tags, container tags) for easy identification
  • Audit trail — every deployment should log who deployed what, when, and the result
The golden rule: if it hurts, do it more often. Frequent, small deployments are easier to roll back than rare, large ones.
Release Management:
Release management in CI/CD coordinates how changes move through environments:
  • Environment promotion — code flows: dev → staging → production, with gates at each stage
  • Semantic versioning — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 2.1.0) based on change impact
  • Changelogs — auto-generated from conventional commits
  • Release branches — for scheduled releases, create a release branch from main
  • Approval gates — manual approval steps before production deployment (compliance, QA sign-off)
Tools like Release Please, Semantic Release, and Changesets automate versioning and changelog generation.
Deployment Strategies:
Different deployment strategies balance risk, speed, and user impact:
  • Rolling Update — gradually replaces instances of the old version with the new one. Zero downtime, easy rollback.
  • Blue/Green — run two identical environments. Switch traffic from blue (current) to green (new) instantly. Instant rollback by switching back.
  • Canary — route a small percentage of traffic to the new version, then gradually increase. Real user validation with minimal risk.
  • Feature Flags — deploy code hidden behind toggles, then enable for specific users. Separates deployment from release.
Modern CD pipelines use a combination of these strategies depending on the application and risk tolerance.

Rollback & Recovery Strategies: Rollback strategies restore service after a bad deployment. Rollback types: instant (revert traffic/artifact), gradual (automated canary regression), and database rollback (schema migration revert). Versioned artifacts (Docker tags, npm packages) enable precise rollback targets. Database rollbacks require backward-compatible migrations: add columns before using them, use feature flags to gate new code paths, and test rollbacks in staging. Git revert + CI/CD re-deploy is the safest rollback. Keep release notes to track what changed per deployment. Practice rollbacks in chaos engineering drills.
Blue-Green Deployment: Blue-green deployment reduces downtime by running two identical production environments (blue and green). Traffic is routed to the active environment while the inactive one is updated. Switch traffic via load balancer/router to activate the new version. Benefits: instant rollback (switch traffic back), zero-downtime deployments, and easy testing in production-like environment. Drawbacks: 2x infrastructure cost, requires stateless applications or DB migration handling, and database schema changes need backward compatibility. Service meshes (Istio) simplify this pattern with traffic routing rules.

# Kubernetes blue-green deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-blue
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
      version: blue
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
        version: blue
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: myapp:1.0.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-green
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
      version: green
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
        version: green
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: myapp:1.1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: app-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: myapp
    version: blue  # Changed to 'green' when switching
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

# Switch traffic: kubectl patch service app-service -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'
Canary Deployments: Canary deployment incrementally routes a percentage of traffic to a new version, monitoring for issues. Starts with low traffic (1-5%), gradually increases if metrics are healthy, and either fully promotes or rolls back. Requires sophisticated traffic routing (service mesh, feature flags, or weighted DNS). Metrics to monitor: error rate, latency p95/p99, CPU/memory, business metrics (conversion rate, signups). Feature flags complement canary by enabling feature toggling independently of deployment. Argo Rollouts provides automated canary analysis with metric providers (Prometheus, Datadog).

# Argo Rollouts canary deployment
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: app-rollout
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: { duration: 2m }
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 75
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 100
      analysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: success-rate
        startingStep: 0
        args:
          - name: canary-hash
            valueFrom:
              podTemplateHashValue: Latest
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: success-rate
spec:
  args:
    - name: canary-hash
  metrics:
    - name: success-rate
      interval: 1m
      successCondition: result >= 0.95
      failureLimit: 3
      provider:
        prometheus:
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{status!~"5..", canary="${args.canary-hash}"}[1m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{canary="${args.canary-hash}"}[1m]))

SAST, DAST & SCA Scanning: Application security testing in CI/CD: SAST (Static Analysis) scans source code for vulnerabilities without executing it. DAST (Dynamic Analysis) tests running applications. SCA (Software Composition Analysis) scans dependencies for known CVEs. Integrate SAST early in PRs, DAST in staging environments, and SCA on every build. Tools: SonarQube/SonarCloud, Snyk, Trivy, Checkmarx, Semgrep, OWASP ZAP, Docker Scout. Use fail thresholds: fail build on CRITICAL vulns, warn on HIGH, and allow MEDIUM/LOW with SLA tracking. DAST should be non-blocking for speed.

# GitHub Actions security scanning
name: Security Scan
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  sast:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with:
          languages: javascript, typescript
          queries: security-extended,security-and-quality
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
        with:
          category: '/language:javascript-typescript'

  sca:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Snyk Security Scan
        uses: snyk/actions/node@master
        env:
          SNYK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SNYK_TOKEN }}
        with:
          args: '--severity-threshold=high'
      - name: Trivy vulnerability scanner
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          scan-type: 'fs'
          scan-ref: '.'
          format: 'sarif'
          output: 'trivy-results.sarif'
          severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'

  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: TruffleHog Secrets Scan
        uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@main
        with:
          path: ./
          base: ${{ github.event.repository.default_branch }}
          head: ${{ github.head_ref }}
Supply Chain Security (SLSA/SBOM): Software supply chain security protects against compromised dependencies and build processes. SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) defines build integrity levels (L1-L4). SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) lists all components in your software. Standards: SPDX and CycloneDX for SBOM format. Generate SBOM during builds and store in artifact registry. Sign artifacts with cosign and verify before deployment. Use isolated build environments, trusted builders, and non-ephemeral provenance tracking. Key practices: pin dependencies to specific versions, verify package signatures, use lockfiles, and scan for malicious packages.

# SBOM generation and artifact signing
# Generate SBOM with Syft
syft packages . -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cdx.json

# Sign container image with Cosign
cosign generate-key-pair
cosign sign --key cosign.key myapp:latest

# Verify before deployment
cosign verify --key cosign.pub myapp:latest

echo 'SBOM and signature verification passed'

# GitHub Actions SBOM generation
- name: Generate SBOM
  uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
  with:
    path: ./
    format: cyclonedx-json
    output-file: sbom.cdx.json

- name: Upload SBOM
  uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: sbom
    path: sbom.cdx.json

# SLSA provenance generation
- name: Generate SLSA provenance
  uses: slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator@v1.9.0
  with:
    artifact_source: .
    artifact_name: myapp
    upload_attestations: true

Kubernetes Basics.code: Pods, services, deployments, ConfigMaps, secrets, namespaces.

Docker Deep Dive.code: Multi-stage builds, Docker networks, volumes, Docker Compose.

Kubernetes Advanced.code: Operators, CRDs, service mesh (Istio), horizontal pod autoscaling.

GitOps:
GitOps is a deployment model where the Git repository is the single source of truth for both application code and infrastructure. Changes are made via PRs, and an operator synchronizes the live environment to match the repository state. Key tools:
  • ArgoCD — Kubernetes-native CD tool. Syncs clusters to a Git repository with automatic or manual sync policies.
  • Flux — GitOps operator from Weaveworks. Supports multi-tenancy, image updates, and Kustomize/Helm.
Benefits: complete audit trail (every change is a Git commit), easy rollback (revert commit), and a single workflow for both dev and ops.
Docker Build Pipelines:
Container-based CI/CD pipelines use Docker throughout the pipeline:
  • Build stage produces a Docker image with the application and all dependencies
  • Tag images with commit SHA, branch name, and semantic version
  • Push to a container registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, GHCR)
  • Use multi-stage builds to minimize image size
  • Scan images for vulnerabilities (Trivy, Snyk, Docker Scout)
The same image built in CI is deployed everywhere — no "works on my machine" problems. Images are immutable and versioned.
Kubernetes Deployments:
Deploying to Kubernetes from CI/CD involves:
  • Update the deployment manifest (YAML) with the new image tag
  • Use kubectl set image or patch the deployment
  • Apply with kubectl apply to trigger rolling update
  • Use Helm for templated releases — pass the image tag as a value
  • Monitor rollout with kubectl rollout status
Advanced setups use ArgoCD or Flux (GitOps) where the CD system watches a Git repository for manifest changes and synchronizes the cluster automatically.

Jenkins Pipeline as Code: Jenkins automates CI/CD with declarative or scripted pipelines defined in `Jenkinsfile`. Declarative pipelines are structured with `pipeline {}` block containing stages, steps, post-actions, and agent directives. Key features: parallel execution, shared libraries for reusable code, credentials binding, and pipeline syntax generation. Jenkins integrates with all major SCM tools (Git, SVN), build tools (Maven, Gradle, npm), and artifact repositories (Nexus, Artifactory). Blue Ocean provides a modern UI. Jenkins offers extensive plugin ecosystem and runs on-premises for full control.
GitHub Actions Deep Dive: GitHub Actions provides CI/CD directly in GitHub repositories. Workflows are YAML files in `.github/workflows/`. Key concepts: events (push, PR, schedule, workflow_dispatch), jobs (run in parallel by default), steps (individual commands), actions (reusable units), and runners (GitHub-hosted or self-hosted). Matrix builds test multiple OS/node versions. Composite actions package reusable step sequences. Self-hosted runners enable custom hardware/software. GitHub Actions has a free tier: 2000 minutes/month for private repos, unlimited for public. Caching with `actions/cache` speeds up dependency installation.

# Matrix build workflow
name: Matrix Build
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        node: [18, 20, 22]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            node: 20
            coverage: true
      fail-fast: false

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test

      - if: matrix.coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v4
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}

  # Reusable workflow call (in separate file: .github/workflows/deploy.yml)
  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
    secrets: inherit
GitLab CI/CD Deep Dive: GitLab CI/CD is built into GitLab repositories. Configuration in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Key concepts: stages (sequential groups of jobs), runners (executors for jobs), artifacts (files passed between stages), environments (tracking deployments), and variables (key-value config). GitLab CI/CD features include auto DevOps, review apps (ephemeral environments per MR), protected environments with manual approval gates, and CI/CD for GitLab Pages. GitLab runners can be shared, group, or specific. The `.gitlab-ci.yml` supports includes for reusing config from other files/templates.

# .gitlab-ci.yml example
stages:
  - lint
  - test
  - build
  - review
  - staging
  - production

variables:
  DOCKER_DRIVER: overlay2
  NODE_VERSION: '20'

cache:
  key: ${CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG}
  paths:
    - node_modules/

node-lint:
  stage: lint
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run lint

node-test:
  stage: test
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  services:
    - postgres:16-alpine
    - redis:7-alpine
  variables:
    DATABASE_URL: 'postgres://postgres:password@postgres:5432/test'
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npm run test:ci
  coverage: '/All files[|]\d+\.\d+/'
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml

docker-build:
  stage: build
  image: docker:24
  services:
    - docker:24-dind
  script:
    - docker build -t $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA .
    - docker push $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA
  only:
    - main

review-deploy:
  stage: review
  script:
    - kubectl set image deployment/app app=$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
    url: https://review-$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID.example.com
    on_stop: stop-review
  only:
    - merge_requests

stop-review:
  stage: review
  script:
    - kubectl delete deployment review-$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID
    action: stop
  when: manual
  only:
    - merge_requests

production-deploy:
  stage: production
  script:
    - kubectl apply -f k8s/
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://app.example.com
  when: manual
  needs:
    - docker-build
  only:
    - main
